newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's ANC urges left to ease ideology.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's ANC urges left to ease ideology.

text.p: South Africa's ruling African National Congress has urged its Communist and labour allies to soften their hard-line ideology, newspapers reported on Sunday.

Two Sunday papers said the call was made in an ANC discussion document presented this weekend at a meeting of the party's National Executive Committee, which includes representatives of the South African Communist Party (SACP) and the Congress of South African Trade Unions (Cosatu).
The ANC, SACP and Cosatu are in a formal alliance which fought the country's first all-race elections in April 1994.
The document warns leftwingers that South Africa cannot buck world economic trends and try to implement old-style socialist policies.
"The democratic movement must resist the illusion that a democratic South Africa can be insulated from the processes which characterise world development," the document said.

"It must resist the thinking that...South Africa (can) elaborate solutions which are in discord with the rest of the world, but which can be sustained by virtue of a voluntarist South African experiment of a special type, a world of anti-apartheid campaigners, who, out of loyalty to us, would support and sustain such voluntarism."

The ANC, which on Sunday marked the half-way point of its five-year term in office, noted in the document that the alliance had inherited a burden of debt, underdevelopment and skewed distribution of wealth.

It said it was committed to addressing the impact of these problems on the impoverished black majority but had to "attend to the concerns of the rest of the population" in the interests of maintaining a stable democracy.
The document appeared to be aimed at meeting criticism from the left wing of a government macroeconomic framework unveiled in mid-year which SACP and Cosatu leaders derided as "neo-liberal".

The framework seeks to harness fiscal discipline, wage and price moderation, industrial incentives and trade liberalisation to encourage local and foreign investment and boost exports, job creation and economic growth by the year 2000.
The ANC document said labour and capital should put their present adverserial relationship behind them "in the interests of social stability, economic progress, reconstruction and development".
